The British actor Patrick Stewart has died at age 86 a statement released on Thursday said. Stewart was an acclaimed actor in Britain with the Royal Shakespeare Company before he starred in the beloved sci-fi TV show "Star Trek" in the 80s and later in the "X-Men" franchise.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/3f9776de-d3d5-11f1-8290-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26302717036908.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/3f9776de-d3d5-11f1-8290-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26302717036908.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">421d404a-d3d6-11f1-b998-9d5338bbdab8</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 20:21:52 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/3f9776de-d3d5-11f1-8290-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26302717036908.jpg">© Willy Sanjuan, AP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Spotlight</category><title><![CDATA['Extremist right-wing ideologies' an increasing threat in France & 'across much of democratic world']]></title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/spotlight/20261029-extremist-right-wing-ideologies-an-increasing-threat-in-france-across-much-of-democratic-world</link><description>
François Picard is pleased to welcome Dr Joseph Downing, Senior Lecturer in International Relations and Politics at Aston University. In modern France, the politics of insecurity increasingly extends beyond questions of crime and public order to encompass deeper struggles over national identity, disappearance of the political centre and erosion of democratic values. The emergence of far-right extremist violence, alongside the persistent stigmatization of ethnically diverse working-class suburbs, raises urgent questions about the relationship between fiery and divisive political rhetoric and far-right radicalization. Downing examines these interrelated challenges against the backdrop of a deadly shooting in the Paris suburbs, allegedly motivated by racist and anti-Muslim hostility.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/0d12be2a-d3d1-11f1-a517-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261029-181811-182756-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/0d12be2a-d3d1-11f1-a517-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261029-181811-182756-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">3fa43294-d3d4-11f1-971e-9b6f2995b8bf</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 20:06:36 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>François PICARD</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title><![CDATA['Extremist right-wing ideologies' an increasing threat in France & 'across much of democratic world']]></title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261029-extremist-right-wing-ideologies-an-increasing-threat-in-france-across-much-of-democratic-world</link><description>
François Picard is pleased to welcome Dr Joseph Downing, Senior Lecturer in International Relations and Politics at Aston University. In modern France, the politics of insecurity increasingly extends beyond questions of crime and public order to encompass deeper struggles over national identity, disappearance of the political centre and erosion of democratic values. The emergence of far-right extremist violence, alongside the persistent stigmatization of ethnically diverse working-class suburbs, raises urgent questions about the relationship between political rhetoric, radicalization and the erosion of democratic moderation. Downing examines these interrelated challenges against the backdrop of a deadly shooting in the Paris suburbs, allegedly motivated by racist and anti-Muslim hostility. For Downing, the attack illustrates a broader shift in Europe's extremist landscape, in which the rise of far-right political violence demands greater public and institutional attention: "This is really one of the first and one of the most serious right-wing nationalist, nativist-inspired terror attacks that you see in France."
 
Yet Downing's analysis reaches beyond the horrific attack. He challenges the political representation of France's working-class suburbs as centres of Islamist radicalism, describing such portrayals as a divisive rhetorical strategy that stigmatizes communities whose residents are overwhelmingly engaged in ordinary civic and economic life.
 
His central political concern is the weakening of the democratic centre. Amid rising living costs, social insecurity and the circulation of polarizing identity narratives through digital media, he argues that political movements on the ideological fringes gain an advantage by offering apparently simplistic, and often divisive solutions, to deeply complex problems. "The centre of politics in France, as in many other democracies, is struggling to hold."
 
Perhaps most revealingly, Downing identifies the deliberate or careless conflation of racial identity, migration status and religious extremism as a particularly damaging feature of contemporary political discourse. By treating French citizens of African or Arab heritage as perpetual outsiders, political commentators risk reinforcing the very divisions that undermine national cohesion.
 
The interview therefore opens onto a wider question at the heart of contemporary democratic politics: what happens when narratives of national insecurity become more politically influential than the social realities they claim to describe?
 
Downing's reflections illuminate not only the challenges facing France but also the wider vulnerabilities of democratic societies confronting political polarization, economic anxiety and the normalization of exclusionary rhetoric.

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Thu, 29 Oct 2026 20:01:52 +0000 en <![CDATA[ Astronauts deploy solar array on 100th US spacewalk by International Space Station crew members ]]> Two astronauts successfully installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station (ISS) during the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the orbiting outpost.

Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), both ISS Expedition 75 crewmates, completed the 7-hour-and-11-minute extravehicular activity (EVA) at 3:08 p.m. EDT (1908 GMT) on Thursday (Oct. 29). The spacewalk began and ended inside the U.S. Quest airlock, with both astronauts wearing NASA's extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits.

It was the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured into the void with NASA's Anne McClain.

Once outside, Menon and Kutryk worked on unbolting the ISS roll-out solar array (iROSA) from a temporary stowage platform. The 10-by-2-by-4-foot (3-by-0.6-by-1.2-meter) rolled-up assembly was delivered to the space station inside the unpressurized trunk of SpaceX's Dragon cargo capsule earlier this month, on the company's 35th ISS resupply mission for NASA.

Menon then secured himself at the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm and carried the 750-pound (340-kilogram) iROSA to the space station's port side, where he and Kutryk next installed it on the 2A electrical power channel. Kutryk made his way to the worksite along the station's backbone truss.

Using bolts to mount the IROSA in place and connecting its electrical cables to tie it into the station's power system (during a night pass, out of safety concerns), the array was ready to be extended. No motor was needed to deploy the iROSA to its 63-foot (19-m) length. The potential energy held by the assembly's rolled-up carbon composite booms was enough to fully unroll the panel.

"And we see the iROSA deploying now," reported Mission Control four hours and 23 minutes into the spacewalk.

About 12 minutes later, the array had fully extended, draping over about half of the larger but less capable legacy panel on the P4 truss. The station's eight original arrays are showing degraded power output as they have exceeded their 15-year design life. The iROSAs, when used in tandem with their older counterparts, have increased the station's power supply by 20% to 30%.

The additional power is needed to support ongoing and planned station operations, including its safe and controlled deorbit, which is currently scheduled for 2030.

Having worked ahead of their schedule, Menon and Kutryk removed some of the beams holding the final iROSA in place on its temporary platform and rotated two launch locks that were used in its delivery on Dragon.

Thursday's EVA was the 100th U.S. outing from the space station without a now-retired space shuttle docked to the complex. Overall, it was the 285th spacewalk in support of ISS assembly, maintenance and upgrades, including 66 EVAs out of the Russian segment of the station and 119 by visiting shuttle crews.

The first U.S. spacewalk outside of the Quest airlock was made by Expedition 4 crewmates Carl Walz and Daniel Bursch on Feb. 20, 2002. The 5-hour-and-47-minute EVA mostly tested Quest's systems and completed "housekeeping chores."

"Being outside, I can say it is always sunny in space," said Menon at the conclusion of Thursday's EVA. "I find it incredible what we have been able to do to provide new solar arrays to the space station. In fact, we have been ... doing complex operations like this for over 26 years."

"This is USOS [United States Operating Segment] EVA 100, which is an incredible milestone. I think it really signifies how much we have done," he said.

This was Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first. Menon has now logged 26 hours and 31 minutes working in the vacuum of space during his current stay on the space station.

Kutryk is the fifth Canadian astronaut to conduct an EVA. He and Menon are scheduled for another EVA on Nov. 5, when they are expected to install the eighth and final iROSA, completing the five-year process to upgrade the station's power supply.

]]> <![CDATA[ 'Crystal Lake' is great, but nothing tops the space horror shenanigans of 'Jason X' ]]> Peacock's "Crystal Lake" takes the story of the Voorhees family back to the beginning.

It's a full-circle moment revisiting Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini), who's the real star of 1980's "Friday the 13th" and the catalyst for all the murder and mayhem. While it's a welcome shake-up to the timeline of the horror franchise, nothing tops the originality of the slasher-in-space spectacle known as "Jason X".

It was 2001, and the "Friday the 13th" franchise had hit a bit of a snag. Audiences had seen Jason Voorhees go everywhere from Crystal Lake to Manhattan and Hell, but where else could this hockey-masked killer go? Screenwriter Todd Farmer had the answer: space.

"Jason X" says the quiet part out loud: Jason (Kane Hodder) can't die. In this movie, we find Jason being held at the Crystal Lake Research Facility in 2010. The head of the facility, Rowan LaFontaine (Lexa Doig), wants to put him in a cryogenic chamber, but the government has other plans for him.

Things go as well as can be expected, with Jason freeing himself and slaughtering military men like they're pancakes at a buffet. Fortunately, Rowan manages to lure Jason into a cryogenic chamber as he stabs her, leaving them both frozen in time.

Fast forward to 2455, when a group of space explorers — led by Professor Brandon Lowe (Jonathan Potts) — discover the research facility and the frozen bodies. They bring Rowan and Jason on board their ship, the Grendel.

While they believe Jason to be dead, they're able to revive Rowan using nanotechnology. As it so happens, Jason isn't dead at all (what a shocker); he was just catching up on some sleep and dreaming about stuffing teens in sleeping bags and whacking them against each other. He rises from his slumber and goes on a killing spree in the spaceship.

It's not the slasher-in-space concept alone that elevates this flick (it's pretty much a running joke that every horror franchise ends up in space eventually). No, it's the brave (and honestly wild) turns that Jason X takes towards the end.

They turn the movie's android KM-14 (played by Lisa Ryder of "Andromeda" fame) into a Rambo-esque action hero in the third act, whereby she annihilates Jason with a combination of hokey martial arts moves and ridiculously overpowered weapons.

Sadly, KM-14 makes a critical mistake: she obliterates the silent but violent killer near the medical station where the nanites reside. Not only does Jason get rebuilt bigger and stronger than before, but he's also now a cyborg with a brand-new metal mask and armor.

Needless to say, "Jason X" fully commits to every eccentric idea and bonkers premise. From the "Kung Pow"-before-"Kung Pow" face-off between KM-14 and Jason to the totally ludicrous and gory kills that border on implausible, this is the "Friday the 13th" movie that you'd dream up after eating too much cheese at midnight.

Most importantly, though, it's never afraid to embrace the shlock and humor that's evidently part of its DNA. "Jason X" is a B-movie through and through, and it waters its roots to grow wilder rather than hide or trim them down.

For instance, when Condor (Steve Lucescu) fights against Jason, he throws a bunch of stiff attacks at Crystal Lake's most famous citizen. However, Jason simply pushes him into a giant drill that's conveniently placed there (where are the health and safety regulations on the Grendel?!).

That isn't even the best part here, because when Elijah Brodski (Peter Mensah) asks the others about Condor's status, he gets met with the sensational line, "He's screwed." How this movie didn't get an Oscar nomination for best screenplay is still a mystery…

It would also be remiss to not mention the greatest kill in "Jason X" — and maybe the "Friday the 13th" franchise as a whole — as Jason freezes Adrienne's (Kristi Angus) head in liquid nitrogen then shatters it against the counter. It's a scene so iconic that even the "MythBusters" became fascinated with this idea and had to try it themselves, though without actual human heads being used, of course.

What "Jason X" represents is a different time in Hollywood, when studios and filmmakers weren't afraid to take outlandish risks with their franchises. Think about it: What else was there left for "Friday the 13th" to do? Let Jason murder more teens who cross his path?

Instead of just repeating the same formula over and over again, these filmmakers decided to think outside of the box and venture into an unexpected direction. Whether you like it or not, you have to appreciate the commitment to trying something new and reinventing the franchise.

When all is said and done, "Crystal Lake" will be remembered as a more cerebral examination of the Voorhees family, but "Jason X" might be seen as the pinnacle of creativity in the series that's never going to be reached again. It's so goofy and silly, but the concept of taking an unkillable killer, chucking him into space, and making him a cyborg deserves a standing ovation.

We're once again left wondering: Why aren't we making horror movies like this anymore?

The shattered planets were revealed by a clear gap in the debris around the white dwarf J1328−1450, located around 1,600 light-years away from Earth. One of the remnants is estimated to be no larger than the size of the average solar system asteroid, while the other is estimated to be between the size of the moon and the dwarf planet Pluto.

If this wasn't creepy enough, this haunting planetary system could be a grisly warning about the future of our own solar system after the inevitable death of the sun.

White dwarfs like the one at the heart of this system are formed when stars around the same mass as the sun run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means they can no longer fuse hydrogen into helium, the nuclear fusion process that provides the outward push that supports a star against the inward push of its own gravity.

As a result, the stars' cores collapse while the outer layers, where nuclear fusion is still proceeding, puff out. This so-called red giant phase can see stars increase their radius by many 100s of times. When it happens to the sun in around 5 billion years, our star will expand to consume the inner planets, including Earth.

The red giant phase ends when the outer layers disperse along with the wreckage of consumed planets, leaving a smoldering stellar core, now a white dwarf, surrounded by the disk-shaped remains of its outer layers and cannibalized planetary children. But this may not be the final death of all the planets that once orbited the now-dead star.

"We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals," research leader Nicola Gentille Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste, Italy, said in a statement.

This system differs from others seen because of the large gap between the remarkably stable inner and outer rings. All previously known debris discs around white dwarfs have been surrounded by single, flat, rotating disks, not a double structure like this.

"The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized," team member Gentle Fusillo of the Astronomical Observatory of Trieste said.

The team thinks that this unique double structure is evidence of planets that weren't completely vaporized during this white dwarf's red giant phase.

That means just like the residents and campers of Crystal Lake couldn't finish off Pamela Voorhees' baby boy, even an expanding star couldn't finish these two planets.

The team's observations, made with the Very Large Telescope (VLT), revealed the presence of calcium, oxygen, magnesium, and iron in the disk around the white dwarf. This indicates the destroyed planets had a composition similar to the rocky planets of the inner solar system.

The team's research was published on Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

]]> <![CDATA[ Big cats, unexplained lights and a floodlit eclipse — 7 skywatching 'horror stories' to keep you entertained this Halloween ]]> Halloween is almost upon us! To celebrate we've pulled together a series of short "skywatching horror stories" perfect for getting you in the mood for the spooky season.

Granted, stargazing may not be the most hazardous of past times. But you'd be surprised how often things can go wrong. The best laid plans can be shattered by the unforeseen, unexpected phenomena can leave you scared witless, or mother nature itself can step in to remind us how little control we have over the environment around us.

Many of the stories serve as a cautionary tale, while others are simply..unfortunate. Be sure to share your stories of skywatching "horror stories" in the comments below for a chance to feature in next year's Halloween coverage!

An unexplained light show over France

And how better to kick off our Halloween skywatching tales than with a retelling of the strange event that terrified my entire family during a trip to France, two decades ago.

We had rented a house in the Charente, with few neighbors and no city lights. It was a stargazer's paradise, so each night we would sit outside as dusk's light faded to twilight.

One night, we stood transfixed as an electrical storm conjured sheet lightning in the distance, when without warning a shining ball of light burst into being on the near horizon. We watched, unsettled as the yellow-red light gently descended behind a row of oaks before passing over the nearby field.

My mom fled inside, convinced that we'd seen a UFO, while my dad and brothers stood and watched as the light silently flitted between the trees before disappearing from sight around five minutes after it had appeared.

We were alone in the darkness, trying to make sense of what we'd seen when a rustle in the bushes had us borderline sprinting inside, all pretences of bravery gone and images of alien greys in our heads.

It was almost certainly a boar.

Our best guess is that we saw some kind of rare electrical phenomenon that night, like ball lightning, which has been reported over 10,000 times throughout recorded history but is still very poorly understood.

My mom maintains that we narrowly avoided being abducted.

Total(ity) disaster

Our next entry comes from Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic, who traveled all the way from the U.K. to the U.S. in the hope of seeing her first total solar eclipse, only to have totality ruined by a series of extremely unfortunate events!

"My first-ever total solar eclipse experience in Rochester, New York, on April 8, 2024, was memorable for all the wrong reasons, Dobrijovic explained. "I was attending the Rochester Museum & Science Center's ROC the Eclipse Festival, where thick clouds had completely obscured the sun. But even without seeing the eclipse itself, totality was extraordinary.

An ominous darkness raced across the sky, while rusty-red hues illuminated the clouds, creating an almost apocalyptic scene. The clouds looked as though they'd been lifted straight from a Renaissance painting. The atmosphere was electric as thousands of excited spectators watched daylight disappear. We couldn't see the eclipse, but we could certainly feel it.

Then, about 30 seconds into totality, disaster struck. We were standing in the museum's car park when the security floodlights suddenly flickered on, automatically triggered by the darkness. The harsh artificial lighting completely shattered the otherworldly atmosphere, robbing us of our chance to experience totality's eerie darkness.

Thousands of spectators erupted into boos, shouting, 'Turn off the lights!' After traveling thousands of miles for my first total solar eclipse, I'd been thwarted first by clouds, then by a car park's security lights. Talk about adding insult to injury!"

The winds of misfortune

Astrophotographer Dan Bartlett experienced a very different skywatching horror story after preparing his telescopes for a night of astrophotography at his home in the Eastern Sierra Mountains.

Nature had other plans. A security camera captured the sickening moment that an unexpected and sustained deluge of 77-mile-per-hour winds toppled Bartlett's Celestron Rowe-AckermannAstrograph 11-inch and 8-inch telescopes, mounts, accessories and all.

"A telescope owner's worst nightmare…Equal to dropping a prized eyepiece or telescope on a cement/concrete ground," Bartlett remonstrated with Space.com.

"When you first see the two scopes lying side by side, no longer upright, your reaction is to stand there and stare. Quick action of prevention is well past its timeliness. Eventually you start to pick things up and assess the damage."

"One might [put] me at fault for not taking down the scopes prior, and rightly so, however the scopes have survived sustained winds of 60+ mph winds over and over before," continued Bartlett. "You develop a level of complacency and no weather forecast in the days of the event predicted winds as high as was recorded.

Damage done? Severe. At least the dented tube of the RASA 11 has continued to win NASA APOD after APOD since the event. Oh, I now use sandbags on a heavier mount."

Bartlett continues to capture spectacular images of the night sky to this day.

An uncomfortably close look at Leo

High winds may be a potent adversary for the humble stargazer, but you know what else can complicate things? Literal mountain Lions, which is what American Meteor Society shooting star expert Robert Lunsford came face to face with on a stargazing outing to the western slope of Mt. Laguna, California.

"I was viewing alone in the local mountains many years ago," Lunsford recounted to Space.com. "Back then I often heard what I thought were juvenile mountain lions screeching in the dark. They were never too close until one night I shone my flashlight upon a full-grown cat about fifty yards away."

"The adrenalin was flowing big time as I kept that light on it. Luckily, it decided it wanted no part of me and headed back down the hill. Ever since then when viewing alone I sit in the bed of my truck to offer a little more sense of security."

Lunsford's cautionary tale serves as a potent reminder that you should always tell a friend or family member when you head somewhere remote for a spot of stargazing. And that you should probably do a little research on the local flora and fauna before making the trip!

Eyes on the stars foot in the ants

Royal Observatory Greenwich astronomer Gideon Bendavid-Walker had a run in with nature at a very different scale while leading a stargazing tour through the Arkaroola Wilderness Sanctuary in the South Australian outback, under some of the darkest skies on Earth.

"I was running a tour from the sparsely used 1980's Dodwell Observatory as our main telescope was out for maintenance," Bendavid-Walker shared with Space.com. "It was going beautifully. I was out in the dark with my laser pointer, guiding a rapt group around the southern sky, when I felt a nip at my ankle. Then another.

Then rather a lot…

I quickly discovered that I was standing on a meat ant nest. By day they're easy to spot: a little circle of gravelly sand with a hole in the middle. At night, they're invisible, and meat ants do not take kindly to their nests being stood on."

For those of us unfamiliar with the Australian Outback, meat ants are known for being aggressive towards any they deem an intruder, have a nasty bite and are named for their habit of stripping the flesh from dead animals.

"Mid-constellation, I abandoned the cosmos and began hopping, slapping and yelling into the night. My startled guests rallied heroically, flooding the scene with torchlight (a cardinal sin for dark-adapted eyes, but quickly forgiven) and helping me evict the invaders.

The tour continued peacefully.

My dignity stayed behind with the ants."

The moral of the story — try to look down before looking up, it may save your ankles.

A relative disaster

There's a long and storied tradition of nature having its fun with astronomers, as proven by Arthur S. Eddington's complication-filled trip to West Africa, as told by Louise Devoy, Senior Curator at Royal Observatory Greenwich.

"What a nightmare....Cambridge astronomer Arthur S. Eddington watched anxiously as the skies over Principe, West Africa, clouded over with thunderous storms," Devon explained to Space.com. "As a Quaker Christian, he'd narrowly avoided jail for avoiding military service during the First World War, thanks to the intervention of Frank Dyson, the Astronomer Royal at Greenwich.

Dyson knew that Eddington was the best person to use the imminent total solar eclipse as a test of Einstein's 1915 theory of general relativity. Eddington and his colleague Edwin T. Cottingham had travelled thousands of miles to secure the best view but their plans were thwarted by every eclipse chaser's nightmare: thunderstorms, pesky mosquitoes and mischievous monkeys from the surrounding jungle who enjoyed tampering with the instruments.

Eddington and his colleague Cottingham only managed to secure one decent photograph through thin cloud. Thankfully, their Greenwich colleagues Charles Davidson and Andrew Crommelin at Sobral, northern Brazil, had better luck and their photographs confirmed Einstein's prediction."

A fall on Gold Hill

Our final tale of stargazing misfortune comes from award-winning landscape astrophotographer Josh Dury, who found himself in a race against time to stage a recreation of a famous scene from television history, with a Milky Way twist.

"One that comes to mind was the image I captured, titled: "Boy on Bike". The purpose of the image was to re-enact the classic scene from Ridley Scott's 1973 Hovis Advert through the lens of Astrophotography. I was hoping an assistant could model with the bike but plans collapsed, so I decided to do it myself.

Earlier that day, I had collected the bike from a local seller and purchased bread to resemble Hovis loaves. Driving to location in a 4x4 — bike in trailer, I dressed in outfit and progressed to Gold Hill.

Arriving before 2 a.m., there were bright LED lights still on. I had to wait until every single one turned off but one. I had to somehow get the bike into position on the steep hill, obtain focus and prepare the other elements — including a lamp and arranging the bread basket.

With the Milky Way moving into place, I really did not have much time. Setting up a star tracker and a prop set at the same time was a significant challenge.

Then, the epic finale. The weight of the lamp outbalanced the bike and collapsed with the most almighty thud (wheels still spinning). I could see lights in the street turning on!! I was mortified."

Bartlett continues to capture spectacular images of the night sky to this day.

High winds may be a potent adversary for the humble stargazer, but you know what else can complicate things? Literal mountain Lions, which is what American Meteor Society shooting star expert Robert Lunsford came face to face with on a stargazing outing to the western slope of Mt. Laguna, California.

"I was viewing alone in the local mountains many years ago," Lunsford recounted to Space.com. "Back then I often heard what I thought were juvenile mountain lions screeching in the dark. They were never too close until one night I shone my flashlight upon a full-grown cat about fifty yards away."

Then rather a lot…

I quickly discovered that I was standing on a meat ant nest. By day they're easy to spot: a little circle of gravelly sand with a hole in the middle. At night, they're invisible, and meat ants do not take kindly to their nests being stood on."

For those of us unfamiliar with the Australian Outback, meat ants are known for being aggressive towards any they deem an intruder, have a nasty bite and are named for their habit of stripping the flesh from dead animals.

"Mid-constellation, I abandoned the cosmos and began hopping, slapping and yelling into the night. My startled guests rallied heroically, flooding the scene with torchlight (a cardinal sin for dark-adapted eyes, but quickly forgiven) and helping me evict the invaders.

My dignity stayed behind with the ants."

The moral of the story — try to look down before looking up, it may save your ankles.

There's a long and storied tradition of nature having its fun with astronomers, as proven by Arthur S. Eddington's complication-filled trip to West Africa, as told by Louise Devoy, Senior Curator at Royal Observatory Greenwich.

"One that comes to mind was the image I captured, titled: "Boy on Bike". The purpose of the image was to re-enact the classic scene from Ridley Scott's 1973 Hovis Advert through the lens of Astrophotography. Arriving before 2 a.m., there were bright LED lights still on. I had to wait until every single one turned off but one. I had to somehow get the bike into position on the steep hill, obtain focus and prepare the other elements — including a lamp and arranging the bread basket.

With the Milky Way moving into place, I really did not have much time. Setting up a star tracker and a prop set at the same time was a significant challenge.

Then, the epic finale. The weight of the lamp outbalanced the bike and collapsed with the most almighty thud (wheels still spinning). I could see lights in the street turning on!! I was mortified."

SpaceX just checked another big box on the path to its 15th Starship test flight, which promises to be pretty epic.

The company conducted static-fire tests with Starship's Ship upper stage on Monday (Oct. 26) and Tuesday (Oct. 27), igniting its Raptor engines while the vehicle, known as Ship 42, remained anchored to the ground.

"Ship 42 static fires complete. The Starship preparing for Flight 15 performed a full duration, six-engine static fire, and fired a single Raptor engine to simulate a deorbit burn," SpaceX said in a Wednesday (Oct. 28) X post that shared video of the tests.

The Ship 42 tests come on the heels of a successful 33-engine static fire with Booster 22, the Starship Super Heavy first stage that will conduct Flight 15. Everything therefore appears to remain on track for Flight 15, which SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has said is targeted for sometime in November.

All Starship launches are worth watching, but this one should be particularly exciting. Musk said last week that SpaceX will try to catch both Ship and Super Heavy during Flight 15, provided the company can get regulatory approval to do so.

These catches are performed by the "chopstick" arms of the launch tower at Starbase, SpaceX's Starship launch and manufacturing hub in South Texas. The company has snagged Super Heavy on three Starship test flights to date but has not yet attempted a Ship capture.

This recovery strategy will reduce the time needed to get Super Heavy and Ship ready for reflight, significantly boosting launch cadences, according to SpaceX. ]]> <![CDATA[ Stunning solar eclipse photos reveal giant hole and mysterious 'smoke rings' in the sun's atmosphere ]]> Newly released photographs of the sun captured during the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse reveal the sun's outer atmosphere in unprecedented detail.

The images, released by researchers working as part of the Solar Wind Sherpas project coordinated by the University of Hawaii, also show rare structures in the solar wind known as smoke rings. Named for their resemblance to the circles blown by smokers, these vortices were first identified in solar eclipse photographs captured in 2008. The researchers had long struggled to explain the processes behind their formation. They now know the rings are a result of the temperature differences in the coronal plasma and spread along the sun's magnetic lines deep into interplanetary space.

"This year, we have managed to capture those smoke rings really well," Miloslav Druckmüller, a professor of mathematics at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic, who leads the image processing efforts for the Solar Wind Sherpas Team, said in a statement. "They are beautifully twisted vortices and there are very many of them in the corona."

The images, taken from the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, also reveal a giant coronal hole — an opening in the sun's magnetic field lines — through which solar wind can escape more readily at very high speeds of up to 500 miles per second (800 kilometers per second).

Coronal holes are cooler regions in the sun's atmosphere that appear darker in extreme ultraviolet and X-ray images taken by probes in space. They form in regions where the sun's magnetic field lines extend outward into space rather than looping back to the surface, allowing high-speed solar wind to escape. These structures can persist for weeks or even months.

Solar eclipse photography provides a unique vista into the processes taking place in the sun's upper atmosphere, the corona, which remain hidden even to cutting-edge space-based observatories.

Space probes and astronomical telescopes on Earth rely on instruments known as coronagraphs to view the corona. As the corona is a million times dimmer than the sun's surface, researchers need to obscure the visible solar disk with an occulter to view it. This occulter, located inside the telescope, has to cover a larger area than just the solar disk itself to protect the images from the effects of diffraction.

During a total solar eclipse, the moon naturally blocks the sun's bright disk, allowing scientists to capture exceptionally detailed views of the inner corona that are difficult to obtain with conventional coronographs.

]]> <![CDATA[ SpaceX's Starfall capsule delivers cargo for US Air Force in landmark 'point to point' space mission ]]> The U.S. Air Force is opening up about the SpaceX Starfall cargo capsule it flew on a recent rideshare mission to orbit — and showing off what the capsule carried.

The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) completed a point-to-point rocket cargo delivery test using the secretive uncrewed reentry vehicle, confirming on social media its recovery of the package in the Pacific Ocean. "With support from SpaceX, the AFRL agile cargo pods were recovered after splashdown," the AFRL wrote in an X post on Oct. 26.

The Starfall capsule launched on a Falcon 9 rocket as a part of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 mission, which lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 20. Starfall carried a number of AFRL-developed cargo pods designed to transport military equipment through space and back to Earth. The successful recovery of the pods marks a big step forward in the Air Force's effort to examine the viability of point-to-point (P2D) rocket cargo missions.

"This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the Future Force," said AFRL Technology Transition Office director Adam Remaly in a press release on Oct. 20.

Photos included in the AFRL social media post show military personnel unpacking a recovered cargo pod for inspection. Each pod contained sensors to monitor temperature conditions through launch, reentry and splashdown, as well as to measure the shock and vibration forces exerted on its cargo.

For its first Starfall mission, AFRL packed its cargo pods with representative items like medical equipment, food ration packs and other military kit that might be helpful for surviving an emergency somewhere that's tough to reach via conventional transportation. To that end, AFRL said it also conducted a fit check of a UNI-PAC III life raft inside Starfall, which could potentially be included in future tests.

"Researchers paid special attention to the electronics equipment and survival gear, including a SATCOM-enabled tracker, batteries, a reverse osmosis desalinator, survival gear and emergency medical equipment," AFRL said in its release.

SpaceX's disk-shaped Starfall capsule made a quiet debut on a Falcon 9 launch in June, and the company has remained relatively quiet about the vehicle to date. Most of what we do know comes from a Federal Aviation Administration environmental assessment published earlier this year.

The hockey-puck-looking vehicle measures approximately 10.2 feet (3.1 meters) across and can return up to 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms) of cargo from orbit, according to that report. And it sports a carbon fiber heat shield and compressed gas thrusters for attitude control during reentry, as well as a parachute system for precision landings.

AFRL will assess the data recovered from the Oct. 20 mission to contribute to its broader Rocket Cargo initiative, which the Air Force hopes can evolve to the transportation of tens of tons of cargo per launch. That would exceed Starfall's mass capacity, but Starfall isn't the only vehicle the military has considered for its Rocket Cargo program.

SpaceX's much larger Starship rocket, which is still under development, was a likely candidate for tests at Johnston Atoll, a remote Pacific bird sanctuary where the Air Force proposed building a pair of landing pads for cargo delivery tests. However, those plans were suspended in July 2025 amid environmental concerns, and the status of the search for an alternative site is unclear.

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket ]]>

On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3.

This wasn't Britain's first satellite, but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow.

The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket. Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

The mission lifted off from the Woomera Range Complex in Australia. While the launch was a success, the rocket's final stage bumped into the satellite after it separated, and the collision broke one of Prospero's four radio antennas. But the satellite still worked, and it remained operational until 1973.

Why it mattered

The launch of Prospero is etched in the history books of British spaceflight. To this date, it remains the first and last British satellite ever launched on a native rocket built in the United Kingdom.

The 66-kilogram satellite launched on a three-stage Black Arrow R-3 rocket and flew in an elliptical orbit that ranged between 522 km to 1,300 km above the Earth. The rocket itself was based on the smaller Black Knight research rocket and stood nearly 13 meters tall. While the launch was successful, the Black Arrow program, which had seen two failures and two successes, was ultimately canceled.

The Prospero satellite, meanwhile, operated in orbit for two years, with regular communications ending in 1973, though it was contacted at least once each year through 1996, according to the BBC.

The satellite remains in orbit today, its legacy such that at least one company - the Scotland-based space startup Skyrora, has announced plans to retrieve Prospero in orbit and deorbit in Earth's atmosphere.

That Skyrora plan, announced in 2021, would use the company's space tug to rendezvous with the defunct Prospero, latch onto it and pull it from space. The company aims to launch its Skyrora XL rocket out of a Saxavord Spaceport in Scotland.

"By recovering Prospero, we are not only coming together as a space nation and taking responsibility for what we have launched into orbit, but also confirming our commitment to the sustainable use of outer space," Volodymyr Levykin, Skyrora founder and CEO, said at the time.

 <description>Mezinárodní šetření TALIS 2024 zkoumalo pracovní podmínky ředitelů na českých školách. Podle výsledků studie mají čeští ředitelé extrémně vysokou autonomii. <description>Český fond Tech Horizons, za nímž stojí mimo jiné zbrojařská skupina CSG Michala Strnada, vede investiční kolo za více než 20 milionů dolarů (skoro 500 milionů Kč) do kanadské zbrojní technologické firmy North Vector Dynamics. Do kola se zapojuje také samotná CSG. <description>Český fond Tech Horizons, za nímž stojí mimo jiné zbrojařská skupina CSG Michala Strnada, vede investiční kolo za více než 20 milionů dolarů (skoro 500 milionů Kč) do kanadské zbrojní technologické firmy North Vector Dynamics. Během týdenních kontrol rozdali pokuty za víc než sto tisíc korun za ignorování značek, telefonování za volantem či jízdu bez bezpečnostních pásů.</description></item><item><title>Opilý elektrokoloběžkář při jízdě po chodníku narazil do sloupu. Těžce se zranil</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904391-opily-elektrokolobezkar-pri-jizde-po-chodniku-narazil-do-sloupu-tezce-se-zranil.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904391-opily-elektrokolobezkar-pri-jizde-po-chodniku-narazil-do-sloupu-tezce-se-zranil.html</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 17:55:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Krimi</category><description>Těžkým zraněním skončila v pondělí v České Lípě jízda devětatřicetiletého muže na elektrokoloběžce. Na sídlišti Sever jel po chodníku a pod vlivem alkoholu nezvládl odbočení a narazil do sloupu veřejného osvětlení. V krvi měl 1,4 promile a hrozí mu vysoká pokuta.</description></item><item><title>Vražda v Jablonci: Obviněný muž se s obětí znal, soud ho poslal do vazby</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904399-vrazda-v-jablonci-obvineny-muz-se-s-obeti-znal-soud-ho-poslal-do-vazby.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904399-vrazda-v-jablonci-obvineny-muz-se-s-obeti-znal-soud-ho-poslal-do-vazby.html</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:36:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Krimi</category><description>Prověrka úmrtí muže v jabloneckém panelovém domě odhalila vraždu. Kriminalisté zadrželi podezřelého, kterého soud ve středu poslal do vazební věznice. Oba muži se znali. Podle policie veřejnosti nehrozí žádné nebezpečí.</description></item><item><title>FOTO: Vypuštěný Vesecký rybník v Liberci odhalil dno. Proč zasáhly bagry?</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904382-foto-vypusteny-vesecky-rybnik-v-liberci-odhalil-dno-proc-zasahly-bagry.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904382-foto-vypusteny-vesecky-rybnik-v-liberci-odhalil-dno-proc-zasahly-bagry.html</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:27:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Vesecký rybník na jižním okraji Liberce, známý jako Tajch, je vypuštěný a připravený na celkovou obnovu. Podívejte se na fotografie odkrytého dna vyfocené z dronu z výšky. Chystaná rekonstrukce zvýší bezpečnost vodního díla při povodních a přinese i odtěžení tisíců kubíků nánosů.</description></item><item><title>ANO přišlo o své zastupitele v Turnově, budou vystupovat jako nezařazení</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/904365-ano-prislo-o-sve-zastupitele-v-turnove-budou-vystupovat-jako-nezarazeni.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/904365-ano-prislo-o-sve-zastupitele-v-turnove-budou-vystupovat-jako-nezarazeni.html</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 12:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Politika</category><description>Hnutí ANO přišlo po Semilech o své městské zastupitele také v Turnově, budou vystupovat jako nezařazení. Zároveň zanikla místní buňka ANO v Turnově. Lídr turnovské kandidátky ANO Jaroslav Knížek (býv. ANO) to ČTK zdůvodnil tím, že nechtějí být zatíženi celostátní politikou.</description></item><item><title>Po deseti letech seminářů přináší Markétina dopravní výchova bezplatný e-learning</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/903846-po-deseti-letech-seminaru-prinasi-marketina-dopravni-vychova-bezplatny-e-learning.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/903846-po-deseti-letech-seminaru-prinasi-marketina-dopravni-vychova-bezplatny-e-learning.html</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 09:54:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Doprava</category><description>Pedagogové mateřských, základních i středních škol se od 26. 10. 2026 mohou vzdělávat v dopravní výchově online. Markétin dopravní e-learning je zdarma, zabere přibližně čtyři až šest hodin a dá se procházet po částech, kdykoli a odkudkoli.</description></item><item><title>Úleva pro řidiče v Liberci. Od neděle projedou po opravené polovině mostu na průtahu I/35</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/904305-ridici-od-nedele-projedou-po-opravene-polovine-mostu-na-prutahu-i-35-v.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/904305-ridici-od-nedele-projedou-po-opravene-polovine-mostu-na-prutahu-i-35-v.html</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 06:32:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Doprava</category><description>Řidiči od neděle 1. listopadu znovu projedou po opravené polovině mostu na průtahu I/35 v Liberci ve směru na Děčín. Práce na mostě nedaleko nákupní zóny Sever začaly v polovině června, od té doby je provoz převedený na druhou polovinu čtyřpruhu v režimu 1+1.</description></item><item><title>Chtěl ukrást maso, pak rozpoutal bitku: S ostrahou se rval přímo v obchodě</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904304-chtel-ukrast-maso-pak-rozpoutal-bitku-s-ostrahou-se-rval-primo-v-obchode.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904304-chtel-ukrast-maso-pak-rozpoutal-bitku-s-ostrahou-se-rval-primo-v-obchode.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:20:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Krimi</category><description>V násilnický incident přerostl pokus o krádež tří kusů vepřového masa v obchodním domě Andy v České Lípě. Sedmadvacetiletý muž se po odhalení pokusil ostrahu fyzicky napadnout a agresivně se choval i po příjezdu městské policie. Nakonec skončil v rukou policie státní.</description></item><item><title>Boulder Point zdvojnásobil svou velikost. Lezení přitom není jen pro sportovce</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/sport/904150-boulder-point-zdvojnasobil-svou-velikost-lezeni-pritom-neni-jen-pro-sportovce.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/sport/904150-boulder-point-zdvojnasobil-svou-velikost-lezeni-pritom-neni-jen-pro-sportovce.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:54:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Sport</category><description>Liberecké lezecké centrum Boulder Point vstoupilo do nové éry. Osm let od svého otevření rozšířilo své prostory a dnes nabízí 2 000 metrů čtverečních pro bouldering. Chce vytvářet místo, kam se lidé rádi vracejí nejen kvůli lezení.</description></item><item><title>Na průčelí baziliky v Jablonném v Podještědí se vrátila další kamenná socha</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/kultura/904298-na-pruceli-baziliky-v-jablonnem-v-podjestedi-se-navrati-dalsi-kamenna-socha.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/kultura/904298-na-pruceli-baziliky-v-jablonnem-v-podjestedi-se-navrati-dalsi-kamenna-socha.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Kultura</category><description>Na průčelí baziliky svatého Vavřince a svaté Zdislavy v Jablonném v Podještědí na Liberecku se v úterý  vrátila třetí z pěti soch. Opět jde o kopii původní pískovcové sochy, kterou před třemi staletími vytvořil barokní sochař Franz Bienert. Originály nelze kvůli špatnému stavu na balustrádu vrátit.</description></item></channel></rss>

]]> Šluknovská liga 2026/2027 – futsal https://www.vybezek.eu/296177-sluknovska-liga-2026-2027-futsal/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 22:03:22 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=296177 Ve středu 21. října 2026 se konalo první sportovní klání Šluknovské ligy, žáci některých výběžkových škol se utkali v Dolní Poustevně ve futsale.
Pravidelná a tradiční sportovní soutěž škol Šluknovského výběžku (dle loňských textů letos 34. ročník). A jako vždy dílčí informace od některých účastnících se škol:

Základní škola Jiříkov:

Ve středu 21. 10. 2026 byl futsalovým turnajem zahájen další ročník Šluknovské ligy. V Dolní Poustevně jsme byli první !!!. Až později dorazil do haly domácí tým a po něm zbývající 4 družstva. Tím náš velký úspěch skončil. Naši hráči se snažili trefit správné zařízení, kterému se říká branka soupeře, a nakonec se nám tato činnost dolní končetiny povedla 4x a pokaždé jinému střelci. Šancí bylo více, ale na ty se nehraje. Trochu jsme zamotali tabulkou svým jediným vítězstvím nad třetím Šluknovem, ale nakonec jsme se umístili na 6. místě. Nutno podotknout, že polovinu našeho repre týmu tvořili nováčci ze 6. třídy, pro které byla velká zkušenost hrát proti o dva až tři roky starším chlapcům. Nejdůležitější je, že si všichni zahráli, naši kluci zůstali zdraví, nikdo nebyl CHORÝ a chovali se v rámci fair-play. Za měsíc jdou do boje děvčata v přehazované, tak jim držme palce, aby naše umístění vylepšila.

J. Kolář

]]> Turnaj Jr. NBA League, 1. hrací kolo divize E – 21. 10. 2026 Šluknov https://www.vybezek.eu/296193-turnaj-jr-nba-league-1-hraci-kolo-divize-e-21-10-2026-sluknov/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 21:49:30 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=296193 Po jarní kvalifikační části (a po divizi F ve VDF) se ve středu 21. října 2026 konal turnaj dalšího ročníku Jr. NBA League ve Šluknově.

Web Schrödingerova institutu:

Ve středu 21. října se ve Šluknově odehrálo hrací kolo Západní ligy Jr. NBA, divize E, které organizačně zajistila Basketbalová akademie Šluknovska při Schrödingerově institutu.

Na palubovce se představilo pět školních týmů, které bojovaly nejen o vítězství, ale především o dvě postupová místa do další fáze soutěže.

Konečné pořadí divize E:
1. ZŠ Mozartova, Jablonec nad Nisou
2. ZŠ Vojtěcha Kováře, Rumburk
3. ZŠ Tyršova, Rumburk
4. ZŠ J. Vohradského, Šluknov
5. ZŠ Jiříkov

O druhém postupujícím rozhodoval doslova jediný bod! Obě rumburské školy odehrály vzájemný zápas s nerozhodným výsledkem 6:6 a o konečném pořadí tak rozhodoval rozdíl ve skóre ze všech utkání. Ten měla ZŠ Vojtěcha Kováře lepší o pouhý jeden bod, a zajistila si tak postup společně s vítěznou školou z Jablonce nad Nisou. Šluknovská základní škola obsadila se svým jedním vítězstvím čtvrté místo, pátý Jiříkov tentokrát na výhru nedosáhl.

Gratulujeme oběma postupujícím týmům a všem ostatním děkujeme za skvělé sportovní nasazení, bojovnost a fair play! Velké poděkování patří také všem, kteří se podíleli na organizaci turnaje, trenérům, pedagogům i rozhodčím.

Jsme rádi, že Basketbalová akademie Šluknovska může být součástí projektu Jr. NBA a přinášet dětem z našeho regionu další příležitosti zažít atmosféru opravdové basketbalové soutěže.
Basketbal nás spojuje!

Oficiální web akce je na tom stále stejně (viz minulý text), nic nic nic a ještě jednou nic. A tentokrát na tom o moc lépe nejsou ani zúčastněné školy.

Základní škola Jiříkov na FB:

Žáci ZŠ Jiříkov bojovali v juniorské NBA lize

Dne 21. 10. 2026 se žáci 2. až 5. tříd ZŠ Jiříkov zúčastnili juniorské NBA ligy, kde bojovali o postup do dalšího kola.

Přestože se jim tentokrát nepodařilo zvítězit a postoupit do užšího výběru, zaslouží si velkou pochvalu. Do hry dali všechny své síly, bojovali statečně a nevzdávali se. Ukázali své přednosti a zároveň poznali, v čem se mohou dál zlepšovat.

Zápasy jim přinesly cenné zkušenosti i motivaci do dalších tréninků. Děkujeme všem našim hráčům a hráčkám za reprezentaci školy, nasazení a odhodlání!
